chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter XXII
paragraphs: Two days later, on the fifteenth of July, an enormous number of carriages stood outside the Sloboda Palace.

The great halls were full. In the first were the nobility and gentry in their uniforms; in the second, bearded merchants in full-skirted blue cloth coats wearing medals. In the nobles' hall there was constant movement and a buzz of voices. The chief dignitaries sat on high-backed chairs at a large table under the portrait of the Emperor, but most of the gentry were strolling about the room.

All these nobles, whom Pierre saw every day at the Club or in their own homes, were in uniform—some in the style of Catherine's era, others in that of Emperor Paul's time, others again in the new uniforms of Alexander's reign or the ordinary uniform of the nobility—and the general effect of everyone being in uniform gave something strange and theatrical to these diverse and familiar faces, both old and young. The old men, with dim eyes, toothless mouths, bald and bloated or gaunt and wrinkled, were especially striking. For the most part they sat quietly in their places, silent, or if they walked about and talked, attached themselves to someone younger. On all these faces, as on the faces of the crowd Petya had seen in the Square, there was a striking contradiction: the general expectation of a solemn event alongside everyday concerns about a card game, Peter the cook, Zinaida Dmitrievna's health, and so on.

Pierre was there too, buttoned up since early morning in a nobleman's uniform that had become too tight. He was agitated; this extraordinary gathering not only of nobles but also of the merchant class—an assembly that reminded him of the States-General—stirred up a whole series of ideas he had long set aside but which were deeply engraved in his soul: thoughts of the Social Contract and the French Revolution. The words in the Emperor's appeal—that the sovereign was coming to the capital to consult with his people—reinforced this idea. And imagining that something important he had long been waiting for was drawing near, he strolled about watching and listening, but nowhere finding any confirmation of the ideas that occupied him.

The Emperor's manifesto was read, arousing enthusiasm, and then everyone moved about discussing it. Besides the usual topics of conversation, Pierre heard questions about where the marshals of the nobility should stand when the Emperor entered, when a ball should be given in the Emperor's honor, whether they should group themselves by district or by province... and so on; but as soon as the war was touched on, or the reason the nobility had been summoned, the talk became vague and uncertain. Then everyone preferred listening to speaking.

A middle-aged man, handsome and vigorous, in the uniform of a retired naval officer, was speaking in one of the rooms, and a small crowd had gathered around him. Pierre went up to the circle that had formed around the speaker and listened. Count Ilya Rostov, in a military uniform of Catherine's time, was strolling with his pleasant smile among the crowd, all of whom he knew. He too approached the group and listened with his usual kindly smile and nods of approval. The retired naval officer was speaking very boldly, as was evident from the listeners' expressions and from the fact that some of the meekest and quietest men Pierre knew walked away disapprovingly or expressed disagreement. Pierre pushed his way to the middle of the group, listened, and became convinced that the man was indeed a liberal, but of views quite different from his own. The naval officer spoke in a particularly rich, musical, aristocratic baritone, pleasantly swallowing his r's and slurring his consonants—the voice of a man used to calling out to his servant, "Hey! Bring me my pipe!" It suggested a life of ease and the exercise of authority.

"So what if the Smolensk people have offered to raise militia for the Emperor? Are we supposed to take Smolensk as our model? If the noble aristocracy of the province of Moscow sees fit, it can show its loyalty to the Emperor in other ways. Have we forgotten the raising of the militia in oh-seven? All it did was line the pockets of priests' sons and thieves and robbers..."
Count Ilya Rostov smiled pleasantly and nodded approval.

"And was our militia of any use to the Empire? Not at all! It only ruined our farming! Better have another draft... or our men will come back neither soldiers nor peasants, and all we'll get is moral corruption. The nobility don't begrudge their lives—every one of us will go and bring in more recruits, and the sovereign"—that was how he referred to the Emperor—"need only say the word and we'll all die for him!" added the orator with passion.

Count Rostov's mouth watered with pleasure and he nudged Pierre, but Pierre wanted to speak himself. He pushed forward, feeling stirred but not yet sure what stirred him or what he would say. He had barely opened his mouth when one of the senators—a man without a tooth in his head, with a shrewd though angry expression—standing near the first speaker, interrupted him. Clearly accustomed to managing debates and keeping arguments on track, he began in a low but distinct voice:

"I believe, sir," said the senator, mumbling with his toothless mouth, "that we have been summoned here not to debate whether it's better for the empire to adopt conscription or to call out the militia. We have been summoned to reply to the appeal with which our sovereign the Emperor has honored us. But to judge what is best—conscription or the militia—we can leave to the highest authority..."

Pierre suddenly found an outlet for his excitement. He steeled himself against the senator, who was introducing such a narrow, procedural attitude into the nobles' deliberations. Pierre stepped forward and interrupted him. He didn't yet know what he would say, but he began speaking eagerly, occasionally lapsing into French or expressing himself in bookish Russian.

"Excuse me, your excellency," he began. (He knew the senator well but thought it necessary to address him formally on this occasion.) "Though I don't agree with the gentleman"—he hesitated, wanting to say "my very honorable opponent"—"with the gentleman whom I have not the honor of knowing, I believe the nobility have been summoned not merely to express sympathy and enthusiasm but also to consider the means by which we can help our Fatherland! I believe," he went on, warming to his subject, "that the Emperor himself would not be satisfied to find in us merely owners of serfs whom we are willing to hand over for his service, and cannon fodder we are ready to make of ourselves—and not to obtain from us any co-co-counsel."
* "Cannon fodder."

Many people drew back from the circle, noticing the senator's sarcastic smile and the boldness of Pierre's remarks. Only Count Rostov was pleased—as he had been pleased with the naval officer, the senator, and in general with whatever speech he had most recently heard.

"I think that before discussing these questions," Pierre continued, "we should ask the Emperor—most respectfully ask His Majesty—to let us know the number of our troops and the position our army and our forces are now in, and then..."

But Pierre had barely uttered these words before he was attacked from three sides. The most vigorous attack came from an old acquaintance—a card player who had always been friendly to him—Stepan Stepanovich Adraksin. Adraksin was in uniform, and whether because of it or some other cause, Pierre saw a completely different man before him. With a sudden expression of malice on his aged face, Adraksin shouted at Pierre:

"In the first place, I tell you we have no right to question the Emperor about that, and secondly, even if the Russian nobility had that right, the Emperor could not answer such a question. The troops are moved according to the enemy's movements, and their numbers increase and decrease..."

Another voice—that of a nobleman of medium height, about forty years old, whom Pierre had formerly met at the gypsies' and knew as a bad card player—also transformed by his uniform—came up and interrupted Adraksin.

"Yes, and this is no time for discussion," he continued, "but for action: there is war in Russia! The enemy is advancing to destroy Russia, to desecrate the graves of our fathers, to carry off our wives and children." The nobleman beat his chest. "We will all rise—every one of us will go—for our father the Tsar!" he shouted, rolling his bloodshot eyes. Several approving voices were heard in the crowd. "We are Russians and will not begrudge our blood in defense of our faith, the throne, and the Fatherland! We must stop raving if we are sons of our Fatherland! We will show Europe how Russia rises to defend Russia!"
Pierre wished to reply but couldn't get a word in. He felt that his words, regardless of their meaning, were less audible than his opponent's voice.
Count Rostov, at the back of the crowd, was expressing approval; several people, briskly turning away from the speaker at the end of each phrase, said:
"That's right, quite right! Exactly!"

Pierre wanted to say that he was ready to sacrifice his money, his serfs, even himself—only one needed to understand the situation in order to improve it—but he couldn't speak. Many voices shouted and talked at the same time, so that Count Rostov didn't have time to approve them all, and the group grew, broke apart, reformed, and then moved with a hum of talk into the largest hall and toward the great table. Not only was Pierre's attempt to speak unsuccessful, but he was rudely interrupted, pushed aside, and people turned away from him as from a common enemy. This wasn't because they were displeased by what he had said—his speech had already been forgotten after the many that followed—but the crowd needed a visible object to love and a visible object to hate. Pierre became the latter. Many other orators spoke after the excited nobleman, all in the same tone. Many spoke eloquently and originally.

Glinka, the editor of the Russian Messenger, who was recognized (cries of "Author! Author!" were heard in the crowd), said that "hell must be repelled by hell" and that he had seen a child smile at lightning flashes and thunderclaps, but "we will not be that child."
"Yes, yes, at thunderclaps!" was repeated approvingly in the back rows.

The crowd moved up to the great table, at which sat gray-haired or bald seventy-year-old dignitaries in uniforms and sashes, nearly all of whom Pierre had seen in their homes with their jesters or playing cards at the Club. With a constant hum of voices the crowd pressed toward the table. Squeezed by the throng against the high-backed chairs, the orators spoke one after another, and sometimes two at once. Those standing behind noticed what a speaker failed to say and rushed to supply it. Others in that heat and crush racked their brains for some thought and hurried to voice it. The old dignitaries, whom Pierre knew, sat and turned to look first at one speaker and then at another, and their faces mostly showed nothing except that they found it very hot. Pierre, however, felt excited, and the general desire to show readiness for any sacrifice—which found expression more in tone and looks than in the substance of the speeches—infected him too. He did not give up his opinions, but felt himself somehow at fault and wanted to justify himself.
"I only said that it would make more sense to make sacrifices when we know what is actually needed!" he said, trying to be heard above the other voices.
One of the old men nearest him glanced around, but his attention was immediately drawn away by an exclamation from the other side of the table.
"Yes, Moscow will be surrendered! She will be our atonement!" shouted one man.
"He is the enemy of mankind!" cried another. "Let me speak..." "Gentlemen, you're crushing me!..."

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter XXIII
paragraphs: At that moment Count Rostopchin, with his jutting chin and alert eyes, wearing a general's uniform with a sash across his shoulder, strode briskly into the room and made his way to the front of the crowd of nobles.

"Our sovereign the Emperor will be here in a moment," said Rostopchin. "I've come straight from the palace. Seeing the position we're in, I think there's little need for discussion. The Emperor has been pleased to summon us and the merchants. Millions will pour from there"—he pointed to the merchants' hall—"but our business is to supply men and not spare ourselves... That is the least we can do!"

A conference took place, limited to the dignitaries sitting at the table. The whole consultation passed more than quietly. After all the preceding noise, the sound of their old voices saying one after another, "I agree," or for variety, "I too am of that opinion," had an almost mournful effect.

The secretary was told to write down the resolution of the Moscow nobility and gentry: that they would furnish ten men, fully equipped, out of every thousand serfs, as the Smolensk gentry had done. Their chairs scraped as the gentlemen who had conferred rose with visible relief and began walking up and down arm in arm to stretch their legs and chat in pairs.
"The Emperor! The Emperor!" a sudden cry rang through the halls, and the whole crowd rushed to the entrance.

The Emperor entered the hall through a broad path between two lines of nobles. Every face expressed respectful, awestruck curiosity. Pierre stood rather far off and couldn't hear everything the Emperor said. From what he did hear, he understood that the Emperor spoke of the danger threatening the empire and of the hopes he placed on the Moscow nobility. He was answered by a voice that informed him of the resolution just arrived at.
"Gentlemen!" said the Emperor with a quivering voice.
There was a rustling among the crowd, and then it subsided again, so that Pierre distinctly heard the pleasantly human voice of the Emperor saying with emotion:
"I never doubted the devotion of the Russian nobles, but today it has surpassed my expectations. I thank you in the name of the Fatherland! Gentlemen, let us act! Time is most precious..."
The Emperor stopped speaking, the crowd pressed around him, and rapturous exclamations were heard from all sides.
"Yes, most precious... a sovereign's word," said Count Rostov with a sob. He stood at the back and, though he had heard almost nothing, understood everything in his own way.

From the nobles' hall the Emperor went to that of the merchants. He stayed about ten minutes. Pierre was among those who saw him come out with tears of emotion in his eyes. As later became known, the Emperor had barely begun addressing the merchants before tears streamed from his eyes and he concluded in a trembling voice. When Pierre saw him, the Emperor was coming out accompanied by two merchants, one of whom Pierre knew—a fat tax farmer. The other was the mayor, a man with a thin, sallow face and narrow beard. Both were weeping. Tears filled the thin man's eyes, and the fat tax farmer sobbed outright like a child and kept repeating:
"Our lives and property—take them, Your Majesty!"

Pierre's one feeling at that moment was a desire to show that he was ready to go to any lengths and prepared to sacrifice everything. He now felt ashamed of his speech with its constitutional leanings and looked for a way to make up for it. Having heard that Count Mamonov was furnishing a regiment, Bezukhov immediately informed Rostopchin that he would give a thousand men and their maintenance.
Old Rostov couldn't tell his wife what had happened without tears, and he immediately consented to Petya's request and went himself to enter his son's name.

The next day the Emperor left Moscow. The assembled nobles all took off their uniforms and settled down in their homes and clubs, and not without some groaning gave orders to their stewards about the enrollment, amazed themselves at what they had done.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter I
paragraphs: Napoleon began the war with Russia because he couldn't resist going to Dresden, couldn't help having his head turned by the homage he received, couldn't help putting on a Polish uniform and yielding to the intoxicating influence of a June morning, and couldn't refrain from bursts of anger in the presence of Kurakin and then of Balashev.

Alexander refused negotiations because he felt himself personally insulted. Barclay de Tolly tried to command the army in the best way because he wanted to fulfill his duty and earn fame as a great commander. Rostov charged the French because he couldn't resist the urge to gallop across a level field; and in the same way the countless people who took part in the war acted according to their personal characteristics, habits, circumstances, and aims. They were moved by fear or vanity, they rejoiced or were outraged, they reasoned, imagining they knew what they were doing and did it of their own free will, but they were all involuntary tools of history, carrying on a work hidden from them but understandable to us. Such is the inevitable fate of men of action, and the higher they stand in the social hierarchy, the less free they are.
The actors of 1812 have long since left the stage, their personal interests have vanished without a trace, and nothing remains of that time but its historic results.

Providence compelled all these men, striving to achieve personal aims, to further the accomplishment of an immense result that none of them expected—neither Napoleon, nor Alexander, nor still less any of those who did the actual fighting.

The cause of the destruction of the French army in 1812 is clear to us now. No one will deny that it was, on the one hand, their advance deep into the heart of Russia late in the season without any preparation for a winter campaign, and on the other, the character given to the war by the burning of Russian towns and the hatred of the enemy this aroused among the Russian people. But no one at the time foresaw—what now seems so obvious—that this was the only way an army of eight hundred thousand men, the best in the world and led by the best general, could be destroyed in conflict with a raw army of half its numerical strength led by inexperienced commanders, as the Russian army was. Not only did no one foresee this, but on the Russian side every effort was made to hinder the only thing that could save Russia, while on the French side, despite Napoleon's experience and so-called military genius, every effort was directed toward pushing on to Moscow at the end of summer—that is, toward doing the very thing that was bound to lead to destruction.

In historical works on 1812, French writers are very fond of saying that Napoleon sensed the danger of extending his line, that he sought a battle, and that his marshals advised him to stop at Smolensk, and of making similar claims to show that even then the danger of the campaign was understood. Russian authors are even more fond of telling us that from the very start a Scythian war plan was adopted to lure Napoleon into the depths of Russia, and this plan is attributed by some to Pfuel, by others to a certain Frenchman, by others to Toll, and by others again to Alexander himself—pointing to notes, plans, and letters that contain hints of such a strategy. But all these hints at what happened, from both the French side and the Russian, are advanced only because they happen to fit the event. Had the event not occurred, these hints would have been forgotten, as we have forgotten the thousands and millions of contrary hints and expectations that circulated at the time but have now been forgotten because events proved them wrong. There are always so many guesses about the outcome of any event that however it may end, there will always be people to say: "I told you so," quite forgetting that among their countless predictions, many pointed in the opposite direction.

The theories about Napoleon's awareness of the danger of extending his line, and on the Russian side about luring the enemy into the depths of Russia, are clearly of this kind, and only by great stretching can historians attribute such foresight to Napoleon and his marshals, or such plans to the Russian commanders. All the facts flatly contradict these theories. Throughout the entire war, there was no wish on the Russian side to draw the French into the heart of the country; on the contrary, from the moment the French entered Russia, everything was done to stop them. And not only was Napoleon not afraid to extend his line, but he welcomed every step forward as a triumph and did not seek battle as eagerly as in his former campaigns, but very halfheartedly.

At the very start of the war our armies were divided, and our only aim was to unite them—though uniting the armies was no advantage if we intended to retreat and lure the enemy deeper into Russia. Our Emperor joined the army to encourage it to defend every inch of Russian soil and not to retreat. The enormous fortified camp at Drissa was built according to Pfuel's plan, with no intention of retreating further. The Emperor reproached the commanders in chief for every step they fell back. He could not bear the idea of letting the enemy reach Smolensk, much less could he contemplate the burning of Moscow, and when our armies did unite, he was displeased that Smolensk had been abandoned and burned without a major battle being fought under its walls.
So thought the Emperor, and the Russian commanders and people were even more outraged at the thought that our forces were retreating into the depths of the country.

Napoleon, having split our armies apart, advanced far into Russia and missed several chances of forcing a battle. In August he was at Smolensk and thought only of how to advance further, though as we now see, that advance was clearly leading to his ruin.

The facts show plainly that Napoleon did not foresee the danger of advancing on Moscow, nor did Alexander and the Russian commanders think of luring Napoleon on—quite the opposite. The luring of Napoleon into the depths of the country was not the result of any plan, for no one believed it possible; it resulted from an incredibly complex web of intrigues, aims, and desires among those who took part in the war and had no understanding whatever of the inevitable outcome, or of the one way to save Russia. Everything came about by chance. The armies were divided at the start of the campaign. We tried to unite them, with the clear intention of giving battle and checking the enemy's advance, and by this effort to unite them while avoiding battle with a much stronger enemy—necessarily retreating at a sharp angle—we led the French on to Smolensk. But we withdrew at a sharp angle not only because the French advanced between our two armies; the angle became still more acute and we withdrew still farther, because Barclay de Tolly was an unpopular foreigner disliked by Bagration (who would come under his command), and Bagration, commanding the second army, tried to postpone the junction and avoid coming under Barclay's authority as long as he could. Bagration was slow in effecting the junction—though it was the chief aim of all at headquarters—because, as he claimed, he was putting his army at risk on this march, and it was better for him to withdraw more to the left and south, harassing the enemy from flank and rear and recruiting men from Ukraine for his army; and it seems he planned this in order to avoid serving under the despised foreigner Barclay, whose rank was lower than his own.

The Emperor was with the army to encourage it, but his presence and his inability to decide what to do, and the enormous number of advisers and plans, sapped the first army's energy and it kept retreating.

The intention was to make a stand at the Drissa camp, but Paulucci, aiming to become commander in chief, suddenly turned his energy to influencing Alexander, and Pfuel's entire plan was abandoned and the command given to Barclay. But since Barclay didn't inspire confidence, his power was limited. The armies were divided, there was no unity of command, and Barclay was unpopular; but from this confusion, division, and the unpopularity of the foreign commander in chief, there resulted, on the one hand, indecision and the avoidance of battle (which could not have been avoided had the armies been united and had someone other than Barclay been in command), and on the other, an ever-increasing indignation against the foreigners and a rising patriotic fervor.

At last the Emperor left the army, and as the most convenient—indeed the only—pretext for his departure, it was decided that he needed to go inspire the people in the capitals and rally the nation for a patriotic war. And by this visit of the Emperor to Moscow, the strength of the Russian army was tripled.

He left in order not to obstruct the commander in chief's undivided control of the army, hoping that more decisive action would follow, but the command of the armies became still more confused and feeble. Bennigsen, the Tsarevich, and a swarm of adjutant generals remained with the army to keep the commander in chief under surveillance and spur his energy, and Barclay, feeling less free than ever under all these "eyes of the Emperor," became still more cautious about taking any decisive action and avoided giving battle.

Barclay stood for caution. The Tsarevich hinted at treachery and demanded a general engagement. Lubomirsky, Bronnitsky, Wlocki, and others of that group stirred up so much trouble that Barclay, under the pretext of sending papers to the Emperor, dispatched these Polish adjutant generals to Petersburg and plunged into open conflict with Bennigsen and the Tsarevich.
At Smolensk the armies at last reunited, much to Bagration's displeasure.
Bagration drove up in a carriage to the house occupied by Barclay. Barclay put on his sash and came out to meet and report to his senior officer, Bagration.

Despite his higher rank, Bagration, in this contest of magnanimity, took orders from Barclay but, having submitted, agreed with him less than ever. By the Emperor's orders, Bagration reported directly to Alexander. He wrote to Arakcheev, the Emperor's confidant: "It must be as my sovereign pleases, but I cannot work with the Minister" (meaning Barclay). "For God's sake send me somewhere else, if only to command a regiment. I can't stand it here. Headquarters are so full of Germans that a Russian can't breathe and nothing makes any sense. I thought I was truly serving my sovereign and the Fatherland, but it turns out I am serving Barclay. I confess I have no desire to."

The swarm of Bronnitskys and Wintzingerodes and their kind further embittered relations between the two commanders, and even less unity resulted. Preparations were made to fight the French in front of Smolensk. A general was sent to survey the position. This general, who hated Barclay, rode off to visit a friend of his, a corps commander, and having spent the day with him, returned to Barclay and condemned as utterly unsuitable a battlefield he hadn't even seen.

While disputes and intrigues raged about the future battlefield, and while we were looking for the French and had lost contact with them, the French stumbled upon Neverovsky's division and reached the walls of Smolensk.
It became necessary to fight an unexpected battle at Smolensk to save our lines of communication. The battle was fought and thousands were killed on both sides.

Smolensk was abandoned against the wishes of the Emperor and the whole people. But Smolensk was burned by its own inhabitants, who had been misled by their governor. And these ruined people, setting an example for other Russians, went to Moscow thinking only of their own losses but kindling hatred of the enemy. Napoleon advanced further and we retreated—and thus arrived at the very result that caused his destruction.

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter II
paragraphs: The day after his son had left, Prince Nicholas sent for Princess Mary to come to his study.

"Well? Are you satisfied now?" he said. "You've made me quarrel with my son! Satisfied, are you? That's all you wanted! Satisfied?... It hurts me, it hurts. I'm old and weak and this is what you wanted. Well then, gloat over it! Gloat over it!"
After that, Princess Mary didn't see her father for a whole week. He was ill and didn't leave his study.
Princess Mary noticed with surprise that during this illness the old prince not only excluded her from his room but didn't admit Mademoiselle Bourienne either. Tikhon alone attended him.

At the end of the week the prince reappeared and resumed his former way of life, devoting himself with particular energy to building projects and the arrangement of the gardens, and completely breaking off his relationship with Mademoiselle Bourienne. His looks and cold tone toward his daughter seemed to say: "See? You plotted against me, you lied to Prince Andrew about my relations with that Frenchwoman and made me quarrel with him, but you see—I need neither her nor you!"

Princess Mary spent half of every day with little Nicholas, watching his lessons, teaching him Russian and music herself, and talking to Dessalles; the rest of the day she spent with her books, her old nurse, or with the "God's folk" who sometimes came by the back door to see her.

About the war, Princess Mary thought as women think about wars. She feared for her brother who was in it, and was horrified and amazed by the strange cruelty that drives men to kill one another, but she didn't understand the significance of this war, which seemed to her like all previous wars. She didn't grasp its importance, though Dessalles, with whom she constantly talked, was passionately interested in its progress and tried to explain his understanding of it to her, and though the "God's folk" who came to see her reported, in their own way, the rumors circulating among the people about an invasion by the Antichrist, and though Julie (now Princess Drubetskaya), who had resumed their correspondence, wrote patriotic letters from Moscow.

"I write to you in Russian, my dear friend," wrote Julie in her Frenchified Russian, "because I have a hatred for all the French, and their language too, which I cannot bear to hear spoken... We in Moscow are filled with enthusiasm for our adored Emperor."
"My poor husband is enduring suffering and hunger in Jewish taverns, but the news I have inspires me even more."

"You have probably heard of the heroic feat of Raevsky, embracing his two sons and saying: 'I will die with them, but we will not waver!' And truly, though the enemy was twice as strong as us, we stood firm. We pass the time as best we can, but in war as in war! Princesses Aline and Sophie sit with me all day, and we, unhappy widows of living husbands, make fine conversation over our bandage-making, only you, my friend, are missing..." and so on.

The main reason Princess Mary didn't fully grasp the significance of this war was that the old prince never spoke of it, refused to acknowledge it, and laughed at Dessalles when he mentioned it at dinner. The prince's tone was so calm and confident that Princess Mary unhesitatingly believed him.

All through July the old prince was extraordinarily active, even animated. He planned another garden and started a new building for the household servants. The only thing that worried Princess Mary about him was that he slept very little and, instead of sleeping in his study as usual, changed his sleeping place every day. One day he would order his camp bed set up in the glass gallery, another day he stayed on the sofa or the lounge chair in the drawing room and dozed there without undressing, while—instead of Mademoiselle Bourienne—a servant boy read to him. Then again he would spend a night in the dining room.

On August 1, a second letter arrived from Prince Andrew. In his first letter, which came soon after he had left home, Prince Andrew had dutifully asked his father's forgiveness for what he had allowed himself to say and begged to be restored to his favor. To this letter the old prince had replied affectionately, and from then on had kept the Frenchwoman at a distance. Prince Andrew's second letter, written near Vitebsk after the French had occupied that town, gave a brief account of the whole campaign, enclosed a map he had drawn, and included his predictions about the further course of the war. In this letter, Prince Andrew pointed out to his father the danger of staying at Bald Hills, so close to the front and directly in the army's line of march, and advised him to move to Moscow.
At dinner that day, when Dessalles mentioned that the French were said to have already entered Vitebsk, the old prince remembered his son's letter.
"There was a letter from Prince Andrew today," he said to Princess Mary. "Haven't you read it?"
"No, Father," she replied in a frightened voice.
She couldn't have read the letter, as she didn't even know it had arrived.
"He writes about this war," said the prince, with the ironic smile that had become habitual when he spoke of the current war.
"That must be very interesting," said Dessalles. "Prince Andrew is in a position to know..."
"Oh, very interesting!" said Mademoiselle Bourienne.
"Go and get it for me," said the old prince to Mademoiselle Bourienne. "You know where—under the paperweight on the little table."
Mademoiselle Bourienne jumped up eagerly.
"No, don't!" he exclaimed with a frown. "You go, Michael Ivanovich."
Michael Ivanovich rose and went to the study. But as soon as he had left the room, the old prince, looking uneasily around, threw down his napkin and went himself.
"They can't do anything right... always making some muddle," he muttered.

While he was away, Princess Mary, Dessalles, Mademoiselle Bourienne, and even little Nicholas exchanged glances in silence. The old prince returned with quick steps, accompanied by Michael Ivanovich, carrying the letter and a plan. These he set down beside him—not letting anyone read them during dinner.

When they moved to the drawing room, he handed the letter to Princess Mary and, spreading the plan of the new building before him and fixing his eyes on it, told her to read the letter aloud. When she had done so, Princess Mary looked inquiringly at her father. He was studying the plan, clearly absorbed in his own thoughts.
"What do you think of it, Prince?" Dessalles ventured to ask.
"I? I?..." said the prince, as if unpleasantly startled, without taking his eyes from the building plan.
"It's very possible that the theater of war may move so close to us that..."
"Ha ha ha! The theater of war!" said the prince. "I have said and I still say that the theater of war is Poland, and the enemy will never get beyond the Niemen."

Dessalles looked at the prince in amazement—he was talking about the Niemen when the enemy was already at the Dnieper—but Princess Mary, forgetting the geographical position of the Niemen, believed her father was right.

"When the snow melts, they'll sink in the Polish swamps. Only they could fail to see that," the prince continued, clearly thinking of the 1807 campaign, which seemed to him so recent. "Bennigsen should have advanced into Prussia sooner—then things would have turned out differently..."
"But, Prince," Dessalles began timidly, "the letter mentions Vitebsk..."

"Ah, the letter? Yes..." replied the prince irritably. "Yes... yes..." His face suddenly took on a gloomy expression. He paused. "Yes, he writes that the French were beaten at... at... what river is it?"
Dessalles dropped his eyes.
"The prince says nothing about that," he remarked gently.
"Doesn't he? But I didn't make it up."
No one spoke for a long time.
"Yes... yes... Well, Michael Ivanovich," he suddenly went on, raising his head and pointing to the building plan, "tell me how you intend to modify it..."
Michael Ivanovich went up to the plan, and the prince, after talking to him about the building, glanced angrily at Princess Mary and Dessalles and went to his room.

Princess Mary saw Dessalles' embarrassed, astonished look fixed on her father, noticed his silence, and was struck by the fact that her father had forgotten his son's letter on the drawing room table; but she was not only afraid to speak about it or ask Dessalles the reason for his confusion and silence—she was afraid even to think about it.

In the evening, Michael Ivanovich, sent by the prince, came to Princess Mary for Prince Andrew's letter, which had been left in the drawing room. She gave it to him and, unpleasant as it was, she dared to ask what her father was doing.

"Still busy," replied Michael Ivanovich with a respectfully ironic smile that made Princess Mary turn pale. "He's worrying a great deal about the new building. He was reading a little, but now"—Michael Ivanovich lowered his voice—"he's at his desk, probably working on his will." (One of the prince's favorite occupations lately had been preparing certain papers he intended to leave behind at his death, which he called his "will.")
"And Alpatych is being sent to Smolensk?" asked Princess Mary.
"Oh yes, he's been waiting to leave for some time."

chapters.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter III
paragraphs: When Michael Ivanovich returned to the study with the letter, the old prince, wearing spectacles and a shade over his eyes, was sitting at his open bureau with screened candles, holding a paper at arm's length, and reading in a somewhat dramatic pose his manuscript—his "Remarks" as he called it—which was to be sent to the Emperor after his death.

When Michael Ivanovich entered, there were tears in the prince's eyes, stirred by the memory of the time when the paper he was reading had been written. He took the letter from Michael Ivanovich, put it in his pocket, folded up his papers, and called in Alpatych, who had been waiting a long time.
The prince had a list of things to be bought in Smolensk, and walking up and down the room past Alpatych, who stood by the door, he gave his instructions.
"First, writing paper—do you hear? Eight quires, like this sample, with gilt edges... it must be exactly like the sample. Varnish, sealing wax, as on Michael Ivanovich's list."
He paced back and forth for a while and glanced at his notes.
"Then hand to the governor in person a letter about the deed."
Next, bolts for the doors of the new building were needed, and they had to be of a special design the prince had created himself, and a leather case had to be ordered to keep the "will" in.
The instructions to Alpatych took over two hours, and still the prince didn't let him go. He sat down, sank into thought, closed his eyes, and dozed off. Alpatych shifted slightly.
"Well, go, go! If anything else is needed, I'll send after you."
Alpatych went out. The prince went back to his bureau, glanced into it, fingered his papers, closed it again, and sat down at the table to write to the governor.

It was already late when he rose after sealing the letter. He wanted to sleep but knew he wouldn't be able to, and that his most depressing thoughts came to him in bed. So he called Tikhon and went through the rooms to show him where to set up the bed for that night.

He walked about examining every corner. Every place seemed unsatisfactory, but worst of all was his usual couch in the study. That couch was dreadful to him, probably because of the oppressive thoughts he'd had while lying there. It was unsatisfactory everywhere, but the corner behind the piano in the sitting room was better than the rest: he had never slept there yet.
With the help of a footman, Tikhon brought in the bedstead and began setting it up.
"That's not right! That's not right!" cried the prince, and he himself pushed it a few inches from the corner, then closer in again.
"Well, at last I've finished. Now I'll rest," the prince thought, and let Tikhon undress him.

Frowning with the effort of removing his coat and trousers, the prince undressed, sat down heavily on the bed, and seemed to be thinking as he looked disdainfully at his withered yellow legs. He wasn't really thinking, but only putting off the effort of lifting those legs and turning over on the bed. "How hard it is! Oh, if only this labor would end and You would release me!" he thought. Pressing his lips together, he made that effort for the twenty-thousandth time and lay down. But barely had he done so when the bed seemed to rock back and forth beneath him, as if it were breathing heavily and jerking. This happened nearly every night. He opened his eyes just as they were closing.

"No peace, damn them!" he muttered, angry without knowing at whom. "Ah yes, there was something else important, very important, that I was saving for when I'd be in bed. The bolts? No, I told him about those. No, it was something—something in the drawing room. Princess Mary was talking some nonsense. Dessalles, that fool, said something. Something in my pocket—can't remember..."
"Tikhon, what did we talk about at dinner?"
"About Prince Michael..."
"Quiet, quiet!" The prince slapped his hand on the table. "Yes, I know—Prince Andrew's letter! Princess Mary read it. Dessalles said something about Vitebsk. Now I'll read it."

He had the letter taken from his pocket and the table—on which stood a glass of lemonade and a spiral wax candle—moved close to the bed. Putting on his spectacles, he began reading. Only now, in the stillness of the night, reading by the faint light under the green shade, did he grasp the letter's meaning for a moment.
"The French at Vitebsk—in four days' march they could be at Smolensk; maybe they're already there! Tikhon!" Tikhon jumped up. "No, no, I don't need anything!" he shouted.

He slid the letter under the candlestick and closed his eyes. And there rose before him the Danube at bright noon: the reeds, the Russian camp, and himself a young general without a wrinkle on his ruddy face—vigorous and alert—entering Potemkin's brightly colored tent, and a burning sense of jealousy of "the favorite" stirred in him now as strongly as it had then. He recalled every word spoken at that first meeting with Potemkin. And he saw before him a plump, rather sallow, short, stout woman—the Empress Mother—with her smile and the words of her first gracious reception of him, and then that same face on the funeral bier, and the confrontation he'd had with Zubov over her coffin about his right to kiss her hand.
"Oh, let it be sooner, sooner! Let me get back to that time and be done with all this present! Sooner, sooner—and let them leave me in peace!"
